title: The table from heaven
hook: the disciples ask Isa for a table spread from heaven, and he prays for it (5:112–115)

segments.voice: Yesterday, kaffarah: the covering of a broken oath. Your line was swear less. Today, the scene that gives surah five its name.

Every surah has a name, and most are taken from a word or a scene inside it. Surah five has been called al-Ma'idah for more than a week now, the Table Spread, and so far there hasn't been a table. It arrives near the very end. Isa, Jesus son of Mary, is with his closest followers, the ones the Qur'an calls al-hawariyyun, the disciples. They've seen him heal and heard him teach. And they ask him for something that sounds, at first, almost like a dare.
screen: `AL-MA'IDAH — THE TABLE SPREAD.` → `ISA AND THE DISCIPLES.` → `A REQUEST LIKE A DARE.`

segments.voice: Verse one-twelve. The disciples say: O Isa, son of Maryam, is your Lord able to send down for us, in Pickthall's words, “a table spread with food from heaven?” Isa's first answer is a warning: be mindful of Allah, if you truly believe. So they explain, and their reasons are very human. We want to eat from it. We want our hearts at rest. We want to know for sure that you've told us the truth, and to be witnesses to it. Then Isa prays. He asks Allah to send down a table that will be a feast for them, for the first of them and the last of them, and a sign, and he ends by calling Allah the best of providers. The Arabic word for that feast is 'id, the word in Eid, and this verse is the only place it appears in the Qur'an. Allah answers: I will send it down. But whoever disbelieves after that will face a punishment like no other. A sign that clear raises the stakes for everyone who sees it. Did the table actually come down? The Qur'an gives the promise, but never narrates the table arriving, and never tells us what was on it. Early commentators disagreed. Many said yes, and passed on reports about bread and fish. Others, including the early scholars Mujahid and al-Hasan al-Basri, said that when the disciples heard the warning, they withdrew the request, and no table came. What the text does keep is the shape of a good table: a need named honestly, a prayer made for the first and the last, and the One who provides.
screen: `IS YOUR LORD ABLE?` · `HEARTS AT REST, AND WITNESSES.` · `'ID — A FEAST, FIRST AND LAST.` · `DID IT COME DOWN? THEY DIFFERED.` · then, large: `A TABLE SPREAD FROM HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Picture a table you've eaten at that felt like more than food: a holiday, a hospital cafeteria with someone you love, a late-night kitchen. Who was there, and who set it? Then picture a small table you could set for someone else: a plate of fruit, a meal at a door, a chair pulled out for someone who usually eats alone.
Ma'idah, a table spread with food. The table the disciples asked for and Isa prayed for, a feast for the first and the last. Today's word.
Your line: a table sent down. A feast for the first and the last. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims know surah five as al-Ma'idah, named for this table; commentators teach the scene as Isa's prayer for provision and as a lesson that clear signs bring greater responsibility.

chat.says: Did a table of food really come down from heaven for Jesus's disciples?
options: The Qur'an gives the promise; commentators differ on whether it came.
Yes, and the Qur'an lists exactly what was on it, dish by dish.
No; the Qur'an says Isa refused to ask God for any such thing.
chat.meaning: The Qur'an never narrates the table arriving. Many early commentators said it came; others, like Mujahid, said the request was withdrawn.
